reviews: Well worth watching and eerily similar to...  This clever plot concept and film most definitely doesn't deserve the term "schlock."  It also happens to be the kind of plot that can be presented very well on a very low budget using stock footage.There was in fact a DEW (Distant Early Warning) Line of radars in the far north of Canada, a component of the film.  Their use in this film, which was released in December of 1958, of the term "Keyhole" as the name for one of those radar surveillance installations must have seriously freaked out anyone involved in the beyond top secret US spy satellite program at the time, that program having begun in 1956.  Their first spy satellite in the KEYHOLE series, KH-1 (Keyhole-1), was launched in June of 1959, just six months after this film was released.Another amazing coincidence which probably freaked out those involved was another top secret US military effort which began in 1955 - the Supersonic Low Altitude Missile (SLAM) project.  That was a very large nuclear powered cruise missile that flew at supersonic speeds at an extremely low altitude.  Because it was nuclear powered, it's range was estimated to be at least 113,000 miles which is over 4.5 times the circumference of the Earth.  So, it was capable of flying around the Earth multiple times... just like the missile in this film.  SLAM's nuclear reactor ramjet was not shielded to save a huge amount of weight, but it did not become seethingly radioactive until started up for doomsday use.  The shock wave from its extremely low altitude supersonic flight would have caused damage on the ground, another similarity with the missile in this film, but not nearly as bad.  Also, even though it would have been incredibly radioactive once running, it would have passed by any spot on the ground too quickly to present a serious radiation hazard.Still, the similarity between SLAM's characteristics and the lost missile's are interesting.Finally, any satellite or missile on a path highly inclined from the equator would, due to the rotation of the Earth, pass over most of the surface of the Earth over time or ALL of it if it was in a polar path or orbit.  That's the other clever part of this plot concept because that's exactly the hazard this "Lost Missile" presented.

Plenty programming (tv shows and big films for the theater) have great quality, ,easy to understand, audio. The sequence where all the action is, where they are perceived to be in the future.. for some reason these geniuses (the director?) decided to film it with a smoky/fuzzy yellow filter over the camera lens..  Brilliant!  It plays a big part in ruining the action.3) Aside from rewinding to try and figure out what they said because the dialogue isn't coherent, same thing can be said about the graphics.. They move the graphics so quickly you're not sure what you saw (and the filter they use on the lens makes it worse).. example: When they went to rescue the 'team' and (I assume) we saw them hanging in the air all upside down (meaning they're dead and can't be saved) the camera shot is so blurry, so FAST you really don't know what you saw.. that's clearly intentional because production didn't want to do a good job making it look like dead people hanging above.. so it's a blurry, quick shot, so bad, I rewound it repeatedly trying to understand what the upshot was and gave up.4)  Charlie (Sam Richardson) clearly was meant to be funny with him being annoying and never shutting up.. but guess what? it wasn't funny.. it was just annoying ..  And the idea he was physically fit enough to keep up with Chris Pratt and keep fighting was laughable..5) (spoiler) it was pretty obvious from the outset the woman giving them directives over the radio (she plays a main character in The Handmaid's Tale btw).. it was so obvious she'd turn out to be Muri..  Viewers aren't as clueless as you think...6) They suddenly move away from the action of the movie (a hopeless adventure where guns have no affect whatsoever on the creatures) and they move to this (what is supposed to be an emotional) conversation  with his daughter.. the convo just lasted too long.. we're in the middle of all this action and suddenly this? . poorly scripted.. . One minute they're knee deep in action trying to kill monsters, then this long portion where he's having a heart to heart with his grown daughter.. it just doesn't work.7) the CGI work on the aliens and those action sequences was pretty damn good. If we'd had more of this, more of the fighting monsters, (and) more of the good guys (appearing) to win instead of the endless appearance of them losing..... and less of the exchange between Pratt and his perceived grown daughter.. Couldn't you have just as easily made it more plausible (if I must find a word to use) that we were down to 2 billion, 1 billion.. 70 million?  The 500k figure is way too corny and yes, unrealistic.9) No men in charge anywhere? All petite young females.. You went WAYYyyyy overboard with the politically correct crap in this movie..  this was absurd how obvious you were from the minute this movie started.. it was way overboard.  The casting aside from Chris Pratt is disgraceful. They should be embarrassed for this lack of casting.. pretty young girls .. you think that's what you need in a action flick fighting monsters? No strong muscular men, no characters we've seen in other films.  I've never seen such bad casting.10) $200 million and the cast is shamefully minuscule.  What percentage of screen time did we see only Chris Pratt and grownup Muri? .. Cast participation should have been more powerful and extensive with numerous interactions and characters that had some value..  This isn't a love story between father and daughter.. or is it?11) Trying to play the woke card.. you FAILED. Aside from Pratt we have a couple women in charge and only other male significant cast (and there's a very limited cast) were 2 black men and a black teen.. Now if you really wanted to play the woke card and didn't handle it so naively why didn't you have cast members with significant roles from other ethnic groups? What you did in this movie is so intentional and so poorly done it's amateur and tacky. Did Pratt have it in his contract he can be the only white guy with a significant role?  How about Asians, Persians, Native Americans, Hispanics, Pacific Islanders.. etc..  ***If you handle casting well, no one would notice the cast layout.. but you didn't, so it was kind of pathetic.2/3 thru the movie the theme literally changes and it feels like you're seeing a whole different movie.. and once again they cast some young pretty black chic as if she's now significant and a strong player chasing down monsters.. She wasn't in the whole movie up until now!!!! and NOW you want to make her relevant.  The casting director should be banned from ever casting a movie again.  This is mind boggling..Look, I give them credit for trying to do a big theater movie production but on a $200 million budget, shame on them for the outcome. ... it could have been worse.. but it could have been better....  Yes Pratt is a draw for audience participation.. but he can only do so much when the storyline and execution is lacking. reviews: Powerful film that explores what it is that makes a soul/spirit  When one thinks of cloning it is usually more physical attributes that come to mind, but this film delves into what makes a person who they are beyond just the physical or genetic material they are made of. At first one might think from the death of her daughter that this is a scientist mother's way of not accepting her daughter's passing, but as time goes on you find it goes much deeper than wanting to fill a void.On the surface it may seem strange and a little nuts to want to do something like what the main character did but she actually expressed quite accurately what a clone is on an almost spiritual level. Those who have cloned animals describe it as creating something very similar with similar likes and dislikes, mannerisms, and ways, almost hauntingly familiar much in the way that a close relative has these similarities that are hard to put into words. They are not identical but have the same essence about them which makes sense given that they came from the same genetic material.Those who thought this was badly written are missing the deeper significance of it what the writer was trying to portray in the way he presented the characters. It had an unusual writing style mixing sci fi with drama and spirituality, and also I think the reason the father and mother came across as wooden is because both of them were rather cerebral showing only occasional anger or sadness. Neither of them seemed like people particularly into children except for Zoe whom both were so devoted to that they fought over her and obsessed about every decision they made as parents. Though the mother was deeply involved in her demanding career it was clear that she had a special relationship with her daughter.It was less clear what the father did for a living, but it was implied that he made less money and resented that and therefore took every opportunity he could to undermine her self-confidence because he was emotionally the more dependent one in the relationship. He still hoped to get back together with her long after she had moved on and found somebody else, but every attempt he made just ended up in an argument with him denigrating her (which was why they were getting divorced in the first place). She still cared about him as a person but was no longer in love with him and it seemed as though he really had nothing going for him and felt unable to build a support system outside of her. His alternating clinginess and antagonism juxtaposed against her rather cold and distant demeanor in return showed that the writer had developed their characters pretty well.The boyfriend's character could have been developed a bit more though. He seemed like a nice and supportive guy, but we really didn't know much about him beyond that.The woman who ended up with the new Zoe, I assume was a personal friend of the doctor's but her character also could have been developed more but instead her entry into the story seemed rushed and abrupt.Other than these few minor flaws I think the movie was excellent, powerful, and made one think. It is timely, just as the previous poster pointed out, given what has been going on in Texas which is threatening women's choice over their reproductive rights; setting them back to what they were in the 1950s. This story presents an example and thus a good argument for why women should have the ultimate right to choose if, how, and when to have a child, or not to.

reviews: A Boy Hopelessly Stuck With the Issues of The Adults Around Him  This film was much better than I thought it was going to be. It was well-acted and characters were believable. It really captured the atmosphere of a back-woods community where people are driven by very basic emotions and there is little to do but hunt and feud over land. As some other viewers have said, the sparse conversation and darkness of the set add to the brooding sense of inevitability that the film is portraying.The one biggest thing that struck me was just how much trauma this boy was subjected to in his short lifetime. He couldn't have been more than 9 years old and had seen more bloodshed and horror than most adults see in 80 years.Unlike the one viewer who said he was whiney, I got a totally opposite impression of him. He was a good kid with a strong conscience, and he actually had more sense than the adults around him who used him for their own agendas.It was clear that his Grampa knew that in that time he instead of the boy would have been the "responsible adult" charged with the accidental but reckless killing of the man, but rather than protecting the boy he was more worried about himself going to prison, and he further dragged the boy who already felt bad enough, into his plan to cover it up, out there in the middle of the night, risking hypothermia, coyotes, and risking himself and the boy being shot by the two men who were up to no good poaching on the land.As others have said, I wondered why the mother allowed 1) The Grampa to take HER son out hunting at a time when visibility was low (she could have put her foot down and said "no absolutely NOT"), and then2) Why she just stood there gravely staring when she found out that the boy had shot the man in the woods and her father-in-law wanted to drag him out there to cover up the shooting. Why she didn't insist on calling the sheriff right then and there and a lawyer to find out what they needed to do in this complex situation is a mystery to me. She struck me as a sad woman who just let things happen around her rather than being actively involved in making sure that her son was safe and cared for. I don't why she deferred to the Grampa who really did not have any legal authority over the child. I also noticed that she didn't hug the boy when he came home from being out all night but instead seemed in a trance with more of that sad resignation she showed throughout the film. It is possible that her husband's death was pretty recent (it was implied that the guy he was feuding with shot him but why that guy was still free is not explained).I didn't understand the significance of a scene earlier in the film when the Grampa said to her that he didn't want to go into what happened with her late husband (as if to imply it was somehow her fault). reviews: Powerful True Story  This story of an autistic boy was extremely moving and it was well-acted and believable. Many autistic children (especially during the 70s when this took place) have been assumed to be retarded when in fact they're not. This is a common misconception and often leaves them vulnerable to abuse due to the stigma attached and the uphill battle to get those in a position of power to believe them when they're abused. The teacher/psychologist in this story accurately read the clinical test results as not a true indication of this boy's ability or intelligence. A savvy professional understands that people with autism have brains that are wired differently, so there are some tests that cannot adequately measure their function. I know this, not only from study, but I was one of those children, but unlike the boy in this story I was not directly diagnosed at age 5 (being a girl at a time when they believed only boys could have autism). The raw data was there but they left out the diagnosis and merely left prognosis open-ended; a question.I know what it's like to be unseen and unheard. I went through both public and private school education and often encountered either low expectations or was told I wasn't trying. Unlike the boy in this story I had to teach myself how to survive in the world with abusive adopted parents who felt cheated but too embarrassed to return me to where I came from lest they be viewed as uncaring by the community in which we lived. There was nobody who had my back and it was very difficult being misunderstood about 90% of the time.With the exception of the pedophile Jeff in this story, this boy had an amazingly good experience in the school he attended and a teacher who genuinely cared about his success in life and, like his mother, also wanted to create a safe environment where he felt valued.Many live-in facilities (up until very recently) had horrible practices that not only didn't help kids with autism, but traumatized them, such as using electric shock as though they were research animals in a conditioning setting, or forcing them into situations that ended up destabilizing them and triggering them. The FDA banned the use of the shock devices but that decision was overturned and one particular school in New Jersey still uses it! https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-care/appeals-court-axes-fda-ban-electric-shock-disabled-n1273572 Many who have had this barbaric practice done to them never got justice against the perpetrators who used it on them under the guise of "treatment" and developed Complex PTSD that they struggle with the rest of their lives. All it takes is one bad apple to ruin one's trust in humanity.Justice is very important, especially for people with autism, and it was important that the boy in this story had the support to see it through and that the facility was up-front about it and took swift action to remove the staff member instead of covering it up, because many kids didn't get that and as a result were left to feel alone, defeated, and angry.I don't know why the makers of this film felt the need to put a disclaimer at the end saying that facilitated communication doesn't help everybody. One could say that nothing helps EVERYBODY, but of course that goes without saying. Even so, technology has come a long way since the movie was made and  this type of teaching does help the vast majority of people that are initially non-verbal. It can make all the difference in the world and communication is key to opening doors that would otherwise remain closed in a society that is based on communication. There are now all sorts of computer programs to help people that did not exist when I was growing up in the 60s and 70s. My communication is way better in writing than it is spoken and I'm 60 years old now. I use my computer for all sorts of purposes now.There are companies that hire autistic adults in some states for IT type positions, but not near enough of an array of vocational opportunities that make the necessary accommodations given that there are always some things an autistic person cannot change in how one does things.I would be very interested to know how the boy featured in this story is doing now that he is grown up and what he's doing now. I hope they will do an update movie about him. He seemed to be quite intelligent despite being unable to speak with his mouth. Some people just need to do things differently and if others have the patience and compassion to meet them half-way the world will be better for it.

reviews: Complex; You could Almost Miss Significant Points if You Didn't Pay Close Attention  Some reviewers seemed to see this movie as boring, but I think the slow pace was done on purpose and not bad writing nor bad acting. It was done to create a somber, cumbersome mood, and it succeeded at portraying the gravity of the situation.Petra, I'm sure, had Asperger's. She was direct to the point of insensitivity, but it was clear she really didn't know how to interact with others and seemed unaware of how she sounded to others. She failed to understand jokes, and loved the only way she could which was mostly expressed mostly as sexual behavior, as she didn't fully understand attachment and developing a relationship on an emotional level.The main character, the father, was somewhat devoid of emotion as well, so that could be what made them a believable couple.The circumstances surrounding the reason for the child's birth made him on one hand feel unworthy, but on the other-hand he felt in the beginning an obligation to raise his child, even though he was completely unprepared. He wasn't a bad parent, just underestimated the amount of work and commitment involved in raising a child alone. He probably didn't expect his wife to die this soon, so was blind-sided when it happened and he found himself solely responsible for the care of his child. It seemed as though his wife did most of the care-giving until close to her death.Although he may have conceived her as a means to save his wife's life, I think he did grow to genuinely love her and by the end wanted her.Petra probably mailed the incriminating letter in hopes he would focus on her or out of anger that he had rejected her. The two seemed to take turns rejecting each other. Often provoking anger is a way that some couples attempt to combat apathy in the other person and remove emotional distance and unavailability even if they get a negative response.The sister-in-law seemed intrusive and selfish even though she couched everything as being in the best interest of the child. She clearly had control issues and ulterior motives. Being a former judge, she knew the rules of custody and knew how to say the "right" things. However, the law was not on her side, and as the attorney advised him, she really had no legal standing to take his child, since he was providing a good and safe home and had done nothing sufficiently egregious to warrant having his parental rights stripped from him. There are lots of parents who are not the best, but also not dangerous to their children and not unfit. They take care of them well enough, and may even improve with practice.It seemed as though she ultimately didn't push the issue, although if she'd been especially vindictive she could have resorted to illegal/unethical ways to win custody. I know from experience that that does happen when a family member covets someone else's child, and when it does happen it's very hard to reverse. I think she stopped short of that line and at some point realized it was not her place to meddle in the natural father's decision.Things seemed to work out in the end. It took some getting used to; being a single father, but it was not insurmountable and he learned to adapt.

reviews: Very well written and realistic depiction of a psychopath and family  This story was really scary because of how realistic it was. If one has ever had the misfortune of meeting a psychopath (or worse; having one in your family) the creepy energy you pick up on from them is unmistakable. Someone like Kevin is capable of playing the part of a normal person when it's to his advantage, lulling those around him into a false sense of security. What tends to happen is that some people are fooled by them and others are afraid to cross them, so they tend to move through life unscathed while leaving a trail of havoc wherever they go that people can't quite figure out. Many of those people never get caught at doing the numerous kinds of damage they do to others. For every school shooter there are many more in all sorts of positions of power who manage to fly under the radar and manipulate everyone to their advantage.The mother in this story had alot of strength to remain in this small town after a public tragedy like that and with really zero support even from her husband. Just as others have said in their reviews, the writer was really effective at showing how isolated she was and trapped.I wondered why her son left her alive and killed his father and sister. On one hand it seemed as though he may have been trying to hurt her the worst way he could, but on the other hand it may have been on some level he respected that she was aware of who and what he was and that she did try to hold him accountable and set limits, unlike his father who was always making excuses for him and unknowingly rewarding his bad behavior. Maybe also he sensed that if his father were the one he left alive that once aware of the magnitude of the situation his father would not come back to visit him in prison because he needed his denial and once that was stripped away by such a heinous crime any support would likely end immediately.

reviews: Excellent Movie About Human Relationships and Complex Social Issues  This movie was really good at illustrating the complex issues within the family and also in society. I thought there was an interesting parallel between the brothers' wife's obscession with having a baby and the first scene where the mother is talking about this with her husband before the car is hit by another driver.I had actually wondered whether the girl was genetically related to her mother and might have inherited her Bi-Polar Disorder but then it was explained that she was adopted. That explained alot; not only that she did not have her genetic predisposition, but also that the reason she adopted a child so late in life was because she felt like a failure in not being able to conceive again.The brothers' wife similarly was not cut out for motherhood because when confronted with a real child to care for she couldn't and wouldn't see it through and instead chose to walk away.The social worker's and school psychiatrist's societal biases made them both blind to the individual circumstances right in front of them. The social worker wanted to try to force the mother and daughter back together even though they could not connect emotionally because of society's pre-conceived notion that a child HAS to have a mother and is best with her regardless of her fitness (or lack thereof) to care for a child. Clearly the mother was financially stable, but her total emotional unavailability would not have been in the best interest of the child. The mother seemed to want the daughter to make her feel successful but really had nothing to offer her as she was growing up.Similarly the school psychiatrist made the assumption that just by reading her records that those previous doctors must be right and that the girl needed to be on medication, rather than looking at the person right in front of him and using his own critical thinking skills. He was very invested in credentials and authority and had control issues, just like the social worker and the mother, but they just manifested in a different way.It showed how too often people's control issues get in the way of making sound decisions.It was amazing how the doctor ended up doing a complete 180 and admitting that medication is not necessary for every child placed on it and that seeing so many children who did need it made him tend to assume when it came to her case. Some doctors never admit this throughout their entire career.

reviews: They can't all be amazing  I'm a big fan of Nicholas Winding Refn (Bronson is an amazing movie- everyone already knows Drive is), and I know what turmoil (mostly inner) that he went through while making this. He was concerned about it's appeal, especially since so many people (as he perceived at the time anyway) expected so much of him now. I think that was all in his head, and he'll be fine, but it puts a lot of what this film is into perspective for me as well as my feelings for it.This is not Nicholas Winding Refn's best work (I love his name, I'll write it over and over- sorry for how repetitive that may be to read), but it is probably his most visually striking film to date. Nicholas Winding Refn has always had a very specific style (inspired by Kubrick mostly- I know). He is quickly becoming an auteur at least in the sense that you will always know when you spot a film he made. His style is so striking most of the time, especially  but not limited to Drive, that people have been inspired to copy the way he uses this style in many different mediums at this point.Now look- this is not at all a bad film. In fact it may be brilliant in it's own way, but it may be a difficult one for a casual film viewer (or even casual film buff) to sit through because of it's problems as well as it's his most minimalist film. It's not wholly a silent film, but there is very little dialogue as well so you never really know much about any character in the film. This both makes it a fascinating study in how well Nicholas Winding Ren's visual style holds a film (very well for the most part in my opinion) and a test in ones ability to maintain interest when nothing is happening or a scene is being dragged out with a slow motion shot for the 5th time in the movie.Again it's not because the movie is completely bad, but Nicholas Winding Refn struggled so much to write the script for this film (which, what there is of it, is all over the place) that very little actually happens.There is a plot. It's super bizarre (as you tend to expect from Nicholas Winding Refn). It's a very thin one, though, and it's told in a fascinating way. It makes the film almost an experiment in the way a story can be told.I don't like to synopsis a film in a review (that's the laziest, and most horrible way to review a story of any kind), but I will say that I am unclear who the hero of this story is supposed to be and who the villain is. I have my own ideas, but the film isn't really one to tell you who to care about. That seems entirely intentional, and in a lot of ways I like this- the way it was told (in this particular film) is fun to ponder and think about. Next to the striking visuals I think I enjoyed thinking about the film as I watched it more than anything.Anyway, I really can't recommend this film to just anyone because it is a little difficult to sit through it. Even though it is short there is very little to grasp or see here. While the visuals are gorgeous (and they are), and there are some good performances, very little actually happens and Nicholas Winding Refn overuses slow motion scenes to drag the film to it's credits.I was also concerned by the way it seemed like Nicholas Winding Refn is mostly just ripping his own films off in this film. Look, yes he did invent a lot of the techniques that he uses (as well as being inspired by Kubrick, I know), but when you do them the same way again in a different film, with different context, it loses a lot because it wasn't designed for that moment. It becomes stale and meaningless.I don't want to critique Nicholas Winding Refn too harshly. I am certain he knows the problems with this film, and he labored on this one a lot (for which I know he did because of the documentary his wife made while he was making this film). I just think it's important to know what you're getting into. Major Nicholas Winding Refn fans may enjoy this film for it's interesting concepts, and overall gorgeous visuals, but it's hard to say that anyone else will like it because it's very flawed despite some (possibly unintentional) moments of genius.

The most accurate part of this film however has to be about Moscow Bureau Chief of the NY Times, Walter Duranty who was really an agent of NY bankers in Moscow and that American business was keenly interested in investing in the USSR to tap into its vast natural resources. In 1932-1933 there was no CIA so the work of gathering information and assessing opportunities fell to people like Walter Duranty. He was a defacto ambassador, CIA station chief, and a bureau chief for the NY Times all at once. He probably had more inroads into the Soviet hierarchy and a better rapport with key Soviet figures than American diplomats of the time.The most important aspect of Mr. Jones, the film, is what it has to say about the current era of American authoritarianism by showing us a slice of history during a time when authoritarianism was on the rise, an era that lead to WWII and the loss of 85 million lives. Americans should consider ourselves warned by this film about all the evil that comes into play and the utter devastation of lives that occur when authoritarianism is left unchecked and undefeated. It made the really bad acting from all three co-stars tolerable, appearing reminiscint of the stiff, soundstage performances from that show, of which I saw every single episode .....live!The story moved right along, and I was not bored at all. It was a very clever script, co-written by Shawn Christensen. Actually, for a movie whos entire cast is only 4 actors, it has to be a DAMN good script to overcome their inexperience.Christensen put together one of my favorite movies, "Before I Disappear." Christensen wrote, starred, directed, and his band did some of the music in that film.Katherine Waterston and Sarah Paxton both need a LOT of work.Waterston has quite an impressive resume of what must have been small roles in some notable films, but again these young women.........I'm not sure about the German guy. He didn't speak English, but I think he just might have been the best of the four.I saw Scott Eastwood when he starred in "The Longest Ride" in 2015. Ohhh, it was not good.I was desperate and rented it on Pay Per View, not expecting very much. There was just a limited synopsis, and it was a bit shocking to see Clint's clone show up!For those of us who remember the TV show, "Rawhide" from the sixties, Scott looks exactly like a young Clint!In the trivia here, on Scott's birth certificate, it says, "Father declined" I've read Clint was a real lothario.There are a few stars that cannot act, who have been lucky enough to have long careers, and their acting has never improved. reviews: bad grammer, etc These women are anything BUT that  I watched this documentary for the first time a couple of weeks ago,and wascompletely charmed by Ridgway's sisters-in-law, Doreen and Tina, and their daughters, Ridgway's nieces, Kristen and Jennifer.I was born, and still live in Seattle.Anyone from Seattle knows the local (unfair) stereotype of the population south of Seattle city limits. The farther south you go, you encounter mullets, bad grammer, etcThese women are anything BUT that, and certainly not anybody you would expect to be related to Gary Ridgway.They all seemed very intelligent, sophisticated, and appear to be sincere, nice women.In the 1980s, during the height of Ridgway's reign of terror, the area where he grew up, still lived, and found most of his victims, was experiencing growth, but had a history of small family farms, and still had a lot of rural areas like the Green River, and maintained a small town feel with a pretty tight knit community.Ridgway's parent's, as well as his siblings, 2 brothers and their families, also still lived in the area.I think this documentary was part of a very worthwile and sincere project. The women wanted to try to do what they could as family, while Gary was alive, to try to get information he might not have been willing to give authorities, especially after being in prison for about 13 or 14 years.They hoped through arranged telephone conversations from prison, they could get Gary to give ANY information, and ideally, reveal locations of the bodies of women still missing for more than 30 years.Kristen, and Doreen resemble each other quite a bit, and it is clear throughout the film, they are mother and daughter.However, I think the director did a pretty good job at distracting from the fact that the other 2 women, Tina and Jennifer, are also mother and daughter. I think Ive figured out the reason.Jennifer (probably married) used the last name Cox, not Ridgway like her mother,Tina,Jennifer and Tina, her mom, virtually do not talk to each other, and do not acknowledge each other throughout the film. They are not introduced as mother and daughter.Tina's husband, and Jennifer's dad, the youngest Ridgway brother, was REFERRED to many times, but his NAME was not mentioned ONCE by anybody.It is perfectly understandable that he would want to maintain his privacy, however, I think it was done for the same reason Jennifer and Tina were not connected.After watching this film again, and some other accounts of the case, I started putting together some disturbing details.In 1982, five women's bodies were found in the Green River almost simultaneously.Dave Reichert was the detective from the King County Sheriff, sent to the scene when the first woman was spotted in the river by two boys riding their bikes.Soon, another person stumbled upon 2 more. A fourth was spotted by another witness, and while at the crime scene, Reichert was walking through some brush and actually tripped over the 5th body. Five womens bodies had been discovered in one month from July to August of 1982.  Four of them were found within 2 days.The King County Sheriffs who had jurisdiction, immediately knew they had a serial killer, and were not equipped to handle a case of that magnitude, as bodies started being discovered regularly.Tomas Guillen, who co-wrote, "The Search for the Green River Killer", said the police barely had time to investigate, identify victims, and follow-up on thousands of leads, because they were constantly excavating crime scenes.By the end of 1983, 11 bodies had been discovered, and during 1984, varying accounts of between 22 and 49 bodies had been found. In 2005, Ridgway plead guilty to 48 of the murders, and is in prison iin Walla Walla, Washington. Currently, Ridgway is believed to be responsible for the deaths of 90 women.In 1983, a pervasive fear throughout Western Washington was building as body after body was being discovered.At one point in the film, Tina is alone, talking about walking home from work around 11PM in 1983, near the area where women were disappearing and their bodies turning up.A guy pulls up in his truck and offers her a ride. She declines.Tina, again, by herself during this recollection, says he persisted becoming visibly angry when she continued to decline. He finally leaves, and she walks to a phone booth just yards away and calls her parents to come pick her up.Later in film, she is on that street, showing Kristen and Jennifer the site.(Talking with Kristen)She points to the phone booth she used, still there, and says one of Ridgway's victims disappeared from that SAME phone booth ONE HALF HOURafter she called her parents that night.Tina did NOT know Gary.Tina had NOT met, and did NOT know Gary's brother, her future husband, at that time.Again, Tina being interviewed alone, recounts when she started dating her future husband, Gary's brother, and was introduced to Gary.Tina recognized Gary, and after a bit, placed him as the guy in the truck.She went on to say that Gary was "a little strange" but she didn't think too much about it.They do not say AT ALL when she met and started dating Gary's brother, but it had to be not too long after her encounter with Ridgway in his truck.This is what I missed the first time, and was confused by:Later, Jennifer is interviewed ALONE, and SHE talks about her mother being introduced to Gary Ridgway for the first time.As I said, Jennifer and Tina have NOT interacted AT ALL. Jennifer does NOT refer to Tina as her mother, OR the story her mother told about  being introduced to Ridgway for the first as his brothers date after her encounter with him in his truckSo Jennifer talks about how her dad was living with Doreen and Gregg, Gary's older brother.They hosted a Halloween party that her mother (Tina) attends as Gary's BROTHER'S DATE.She encounters a man in a long hooded cape and a green mask. He is introduced as her date's brother, Gary.The cape and hood had leaves, and twigs taped all over it. Jennifer recounts that her mother asks him who he is supposed to be. He answers, "I'm "The Riverman", a name Ted Bundy coined for "The Green River Killer"After watching the first time, even though there were only three brothers, I was confused about Jennifer's parentage.Now, Tina, recounting first being introduced to Gary as her date and future husbands brother, WITHOUT mentioning the little detail that it was at a Halloween party where Ridgway was dressed as the Green River Killer, had basically tried to abduct her, and just saying he was "kind of strange but didn't think much more about it" sounds like a lie, sadly.By Tina and Jennifer not interacting at all, NOT being clearly identified as mother and daughter, Gary's younger brother, Jennifer's dad and Tina's husband,  never being referred to by name, by Tina especially, was all done on purpose, to make Tina and Jennifer's accounts sound like two different stories about 2 different people.Doreen, Kristen's mom DID briefly admit that there were signs that Gary could be the killer, but she was in denialHowever, the main theme, and by all accounts of the family, including Tina and Jennifer, Ridgway was the poster boy for the nice family man.In the beginning of the film, Kristen talks about how Ridgway not only ripped apart the victims' families, but their own family as well. She goes on to say the the four women hadn't been together in ten years, after being, by their accounts, a very close, happy family.Kristen said when Gary was arrested in 2002, she was in a terrible state, hiding out, ashamed of her name, ashamed to share his DNA.The whole Ridgway family had lived in that small community for well over 50 years. It must have been devastating on so many levels.I don't think it would be possible for Tina, especially, to participate in the film and not talk about her encounter with Ridgway. The story about her first introduction to him in his Halloween costume being told by Tina would leave glaring questions, but is too good to leave out, so they try to distract that the Halloween story is about her.I cannot imagine continuing to date a guy whose brother had tried to abduct me, during a time a serial killer, the most prolific in US history, is operating in my neighborhood, or not reporting him to the police.Why has the Ridgway family been, "ripped apart", as Kristen said. They had a history of being very close. Adversity CAN bring people closer. Why did it not in this already close family?Gary was an early suspect in the GRK, but they lacked hard evidence, and after being arrested twice for solicitation, in 1987, he agreed to take a lie detector test...... and passed. SO did Ted Bundy. Ridgway was shelved.What I wonder is who knew about Tina's encounter with Gary?  Did Tina keep it to herself? Did she tell his brother? Maybe there was a family decision to keep it quiet. Maybe SOME knew. Maybe others didn't find out until it was too late, and have to live with a responsibility for lost lives.........I think there is another story about the Ridgway family that could prove quite intetesting.

reviews: The Computer Science / Math is 95% wrong  I wanted to like this movie. I'm a computer scientist who works on NP complete problems in my research. The premise of the film attracted me to watch it. However, the writers should have sought experts as consultants. They clearly did not as they got the theory of NP completeness almost entirely wrong.The major flaw is that the 4 mathematicians who are portrayed as having solved the question of whether or not P=NP, rely on what they describe as a nondeterministic machine in their supposed proof that P is equal to NP. Although the N in NP means nondeterministic,  the theory of NP completeness assumes a Turing Machine, which is deterministic.  Although they don't use the term quantum computer in the movie, what they describe as their nondeterministic machine must be a quantum computer.  Quantum computers are not Turing Machines.  Solving an NP complete problem in polynomial time on a quantum computer does NOT prove P is equal to NP.They did get something right though.  If P is ever proved equal to NP, then the ramifications of that on cryptography, science, etc are as explained by the 4 mathematician characters. reviews: Contrived discomfort and bleakness  I make it a point to watch the entire movie if I want to review it. For this reason, I watched C.O.G. to the very end.  The movie gives the viewer many reasons to want to hit the stop button and little reason to continue watching.  In tone, this work is insulting to the communities that the main character encounters.  In addition, the very premise of the the movie is problematic: a graduate student of Yale wishes to experience hardship, somewhat inanely, among various communities in Oregon: Farmers, factory and migrant workers, evangelizing christians, are conceived here as the unwashed, ignorant, bigoted, and unprogressive poor. In the eyes of this young man, their belief systems are a blight on life in general and a source of distress for him in particular. However, being apparently helpless against the ignorant masses, he has no answers and nor will he terminate his voluntary foray into their lives.  So he just suffers among them for the duration of his planned time there.  He doesn't start to understand this life differently and they never start to see him differently.The writing labors. A lot of bad language is employed, and crass humor abounds.  Throughout the shoddy plot, much contrived discomfort is suffered.  The acting is poor, the settings unnecessarily bleak.  Although the issues are current (gay rights, underserved populations, etc), they are so ineptly handled as to leave the viewer feeling frustrated at all else that could have been said, done, understood, learned.In the end, the impression one gets is that ultimately, there is little of value in this negative and deficient work.

reviews: Doesn't do Mr. Paulides cause justice  As an avid listeners to David Paulides interviews and viewers of his Youtube channel, my friend and I were excited to finally watch this together.  Paulides is a thorough and thoughtful investigator with strong credibility and a deep compassion for the victims.  He's also a great speaker and presents evidence very well, particularly the patterns and similarities between cases that make up the evidence that is Missing 411.  He's wonderful at connecting the dots for the listener/reader but careful to walk the line of allowing you to come up with your own theory.  He's long been guarded of what his theory behind the vast collection of abnormal National Parks Missing Person Cases is.  None of that was present in this film.  I know he teamed up with his son to make this film and I have to say it was beautiful shot.  The footage/camera work is gorgeous, as is the lighting and sound quality.  The problem is that nothing is presented.  For some reason the cases explored are all male children, which makes no sense given Mr. Paulides normally presents cases of both genders of all ages.  They don't talk about the patterns or even present that material.  Nothing about water, boulder fields, being the last person in a row of hikers, etc.  It's really strange that they left that out.  It feels more like a Dateline episode as it focuses primarily on one case which the details of are told again and again and again, while intercutting other stories. All the cases they presented are easily dismissed as being the fault of negligent adults who weren't watching the small children properly.  One even includes a mentally challenged pedophile former convict, so you can't help but assume he did something awful.  That particular child also has a creepy Great-Grandfather who refers to the missing 2 year old consistently as "the kid" and laughs frequently while answering questions about his disappearance.  Further, the Great-Grandfather refuses to be on camera.  WTF?  It's also strange that they focused on cases where the families were all of rural-lower-socio-economic circumstances.  You'd think they would have used more of a cross-section.  Basically it feels like they could only get these few families to agree to be interviewed and so they made the movie with the footage they had instead of taking the time to get more interviews so it was a stronger thesis.  I hope they will make another movie and will fix these issues.  I feel terrible for all of the parents/families who have lost someone and Mr. Paulides work is so important.  He's a wonderful person with a strong-skillset and the ability to draw attention to his cause.  I just don't think this movie is doing that.  I really hope they will get more interviews about missing adults and recut this film with that new footage and make a sequel that includes all of the patterns of these cases, as well as all of his tips for how to avoid going missing.  Also, it was very hard to follow who was who and which case they belonged to.  It would have been nice to have names appear on screen each time a talking head reappeared. I found that peculiar but then thought about the fact this was probably made before she starred in her hit movies.It's not a thrill or exciting and there's no real big build up (and subsequent overflow) of anything. Most movies and well, stories for that matter, have climaxes near the end. This one has....struggles and revelations. Those are dealt with as they occur.I'm gonna tell you what I liked most about this movie. It wasn't the usual troupe of the unfortunate, underprivileged black woman that is cursed to work for the spoiled, cruel southern white woman and she has to set her straight about "the real world".The story works out that this could have easily been so but the movie actually dealt with the way real life is here in the modern world. They were two women from different worlds, who didn't even necessarily fit into their own worlds, but weren't bitter about it either. Both of them equally had to be real with each other or it wasn't going to work. They both needed each other and deep down they knew it. That's why they made it work. Because of that, it did work and they got along like actual human beings get along in the real world.Don't get me wrong, they did point out the two local southern women that came to visit her and boy were they on point! They were so on point about everything we hate about the South I had to laugh (I can say that as I'm a Southerner). You could cut the overly proper, controlling passive-aggressiveness with a knife! This is the kicker of why I liked that; it showed these two women as only a PART of the South, not the South. There is so much more to us than what Hollywood would love you to think sometimes. This movie displayed that.The lady in this film had been around, and she accepted nothing less than straight forwardness, and yet at the same time was not going to be bossed around. She was used to being independent and yet as a  movie star she had some "spoiled" issues that she had to face. The "black servant" role (or whatever you'd like to call it - she wasn't a "servant" in this movie) had to show her this and teach her about this certain type of hardship, but it wasn't because of race. It was because of her own life experiences (which gets revealed later of course). It wasn't a black to white kind of thing, it was a human to human thing.I'm baffled as to how Hollywood could have made such a REAL movie and stayed oh so slightly away from the temptation to make race, sex, sexual orientation, religion, etc an issue (and all of this was there to play with as they usually do).This a very mature movie for mature people with a head on their shoulders and an attention span of more than a couple of minutes. If you are over all the social issues Hollywood still thinks to this day you need to be preached to about, and want to cut through the crap and appreciate a movie about relationships between human beings, this will be one of your go to's.As others have pointed out, I thought the ending was kind of abrupt. But maybe that's in keeping with the them of the movie. What else was there supposed to be? Running off into the sunset with flowers in their hair?

Theodore Roosevelt comes quickly to mind â an ardent hunter and an ardent conservationist.Now to questions raised. First, do bears see human beings as prey animals? Not normally, but an old bear that cannot hunt strong or fast prey might see a human as a potential meal. I think that is what happened to Timothy Treadwell and his girlfriend, but I did not follow that closely. Another exception may be made for the polar bear. To a polar bear, any other creature is a potential meal. Second, have there been unprovoked attacks on humans? Yes. On two consecutive nights in 1967 in Glacier National Park, two sleeping young women, miles apart, were dragged from their tents, mauled, and partially eaten by grizzly bears, and a young man was injured but not killed. Further, look up the account of the friend of a man who raised and trained a grizzly bear. The friend was assured that he could stand close to the bear who was not a danger. Suddenly, for no obvious reason, the bear attacked the friend who subsequently died from the attack. I saw a video of the attack and it was chilling. When Eliza takes a morning bath, she immerses herself into the water, and we are immersed into her morning routine, which includes masturbation in the bath tub, as well as boiling eggs. Her father lives with her and is an artist and ostensibly homosexual, trying to hit on the waiter in the local pie shop. The plot revolves around the discovery of the Creature of The Black Lagoon, for lack of a better term, and the capture and scientific analysis of the creature that some locals in the Amazon believe is a God. We have the perfect storm - a collision of Russians, trying to steal the creature, Eliza who is love with the creature, and the US government hellbent on destroying it to analyze its biological functions, All of this is set in the early sixties (I believe) and the movie does a good job of showing how people lived and interacted during that time period. The plot is a simplistic one, revolving around the capture and rescue of the creature, and the tone is one of love for someone different (outsiders) than the normal daily routine of  everyday life and relationships. There are some racial overtones, misogyny, and the bullheaded people who work for the military. Water is displayed throughout the movie and is a symbol for rebirth, or possibly a transformative element.  I won't spoil the ending, you'll have to watch the movie and I highly recommend that you do. reviews: A Great Movie  This is a dystopian film based in the future (2027) in England. The story line is to get a pregnant girl to the Human Project in a world where infertility has left humans without children, and possible human extinction. The movie is set in a world where the rich have isolated themselves from the rest of the world, were pills and video games rule their day.  The poor are left to survive in a world with pollution, dirty water, filthy air, and lack of food, surrounded by intense overpopulation, immigration, anarchy and basic tribalism.  Terrorism hits home as the main character, Clive Owen, (Theo) just misses an explosion at a coffee shop on his way to work. The police have militarized and use extensive force to round up immigrants and deport them, sometimes in a brutal manner. As the world reels from the weight of these problems, Britain soldiers on. When the youngest person, Baby Diego, dies at the hands of a fanatic, the world mourns his death, the weight of hopelessness settles in and creates an atmosphere of gloom and no possible future for humanity. The pregnant girl happens to be an immigrant which adds a twist of irony to the film, since the English government is rounding up and deporting immigrants in a brutal and efficient manner. The movie is filmed with dark colors with lots of gray tones surrounded by an atmosphere of damp and wet surroundings.An activist group lures Theo into getting transient papers to move this pregnant girl to the Human Project, the last bastion of hope for the human race since governments can no longer be trusted, and the activists don't trust one another, and the proverbial uprising is always around the corner, never fully getting a start, as the government and the police squash any hope of resolving societies ills. But through all of the chaos, Theo manages to get this pregnant girl to her rendezvous by a buoy in the ocean.  Some of the main ideas in this movie are relevant in today's world, especially England.  The themes of immigration, terrorism, militarized police forces, government surveillance, anarchy, and activism are salient issues found throughout the civilized world. Overpopulation, pollution, Global Climate change, are featured in the movie as well. But out of the fog comes the boat, Tomorrow, to rescue the pregnant girl.The movie never asks why the human race has stopped reproducing, an issue about the science that once helped humanity, is now lost in the hopelessness that pervades the landscape. This movie has a strong message about issues that are going on in today's world. What is evident is that the groups of people in the movie have assembled into tribes, for lack of a better word.  The government and the police versus the anarchists and the activists. The activists rying to get the baby to the Human Project and fight with each other.  The terrorists fighting the police forces, and the immigrants herding animals into their living quarters.  All great civilizations have one thing in common - they were organized, designed and built by the group of people with the dominant gene. They were also undermined through immigration, when the lesser gene moved into their cities, and began to mix their cultures, leading to the fall of that society.  A perfect example is Rome. Whether you want to believe it or not, society is a racial construct.

Of course, this is really about man using science to stay alive, while battling one of the most inhospitable places for humans - space. The pressure on Mars is 150 that of earth (14.7 psi), and the pressure on Mars would kill a human in approximately one minute, when fully exposed.  It was interesting to see the pressure, temperature, and oxygen icons displayed on his instruments.  Very spaceadelic, indeed. I also noticed how China helped the NASA in this film, but this is inaccurate, due to obvious security concerns, and from a personal nature, their technology is horrible, and they still produce junk, and I think it would hamper our rescue efforts if indeed this was the case. Another aspect of the movie that was right on, was the structure of government, with bureaucrats running the show, like the Alpha Male, (Jeff Daniels - excellent performance) bowing to his superiors and so on down the line.  I also liked the young astrodynamics student, with no social skills, trying to explain his theory for the rescue attempt. Overall, a definite go see, and it will keep you on the edge of your seat the entire time you are viewing it.

reviews: Wholesome and uplifting  "The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much." (James 5:16b)"Verily I say unto you, except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 18:3)Those two Bible verses perfectly encapsulate what this film is all about, in a way that the 1990's remake (which I grew up with) was not. More generally, it is a good example of the difference between old-school and modern Disney. Once upon a time, Disney stood for and provided wholesome entertainment that promoted family values and moral uplift. Now they just seek to provide entertainment for its own sake (or other things which I don't need to elaborate). And it's not new. This has been going on for at least 30 years. All that aside, I found this film to be outstanding. It is simple, yes, and the conclusion is telegraphed from the very beginning, but it understands that a child's sense of wonder and ease of belief are laudable things that should be protected instead of dismissed out of hand or reasoned away. It also shows the possibility and power of redemption. All of these are reason enough for me to return to this again instead of the remake, entertaining as it may be.

reviews: Last but not least  As the last of the Astaire/Rogers films (and the only one in color), this was always going to be bittersweet. Never again will I be able to watch these gems for the first time. They have been able to transport me to another world in a way that few other films can, and for that I will always be grateful. The plot this time, different from the others (except Vernon and Irene Castle) has the duo already being married, falling out of love, and finding each other again, which seemed very appropriate for them at this stage in their careers. I don't think one should read too much into this metatextually, but the parallels are still there. For me, the best numbers were 'My One and Only Highland Fling' and 'They Can't Take That Away from Me'; the former for its elegant simplicity and "cute" factor; the latter for its lush romantic quality, recalling the best of their 1930's output. In terms of the whole body of work, it's somewhere in the middle, but I'd be lying if I said I didn't have a lovely time. And before I forget, while Astaire and Rogers were the main course, Oscar Levant was a tasy side dish.

reviews: Steven Seagal is: The Punisher (sort of)  Ugh. It's a foregone conclusion that Seagal will never make anything again that lives up to his heyday in the 80's and 90's, but at least his DTV work up to this point had been quirkily interesting. As Seagal has aged and grown more portly, he's done less hand-to-hand combat and relied more on guns and knives, but the new trend seems to be that he barely appears in movies where he has the top billing. SNIPER: SPECIAL OPS was guilty of this, but at least that one had the good sense to be on the short and simple side. CODE OF HONOR is, quite frankly, one of the most cynical and shoddy pieces of work (and I use the term loosely) to ever have Seagal's name slapped onto it. Here, he plays Colonel Robert Sikes, a Punisher-like character who acts as a vigilante in his city to clean up crime. On his trail is a former protÃ©gÃ©/friend who is trying to bring him in along with the help of the police. And, for some reason, there is a sleazy news team who follow them around trying to get a good story. So, you have elements of THE PUNISHER, SURVIVOR (the generic Pierce Brosnan movie from last year), and NIGHTCRAWLER, with none of the nuance or sophistication of each (at least the first and last ones). There are no characters with significant screen time to root for, as government, the police, and news media are all painted in such a bad way. Even Seagal who normally is likeable, if stoic, is stuck playing a character who straight up murders people. Of course, I was with the movie for about two-thirds of it because it was kind of entertaining in a bad way. However, a third act plot twist completely ruined the film for me. It's like the filmmakers/screenwriter were like, "Just kidding!" It honestly angered me a little bit, making the last half hour or so a real chore to get through. As for the action, which is what most people will care about, there is a decent amount of it although it's mostly shootouts and some knife-fighting. Seagal gets very little to do, and I was disappointed here just like with SNIPER: SPECIAL OPS. The opening scene was probably the best, and there was a couple short fight scenes towards the end that partially made up for how dismal the rest of the film was. Seagal also gets one of his trademark speeches about halfway through, although the politics of it rubbed me the wrong way. Ultimately, I feel like I've been tested for the last time as a Seagal fan. These last two films were a whole new level of lazy, and I don't know if I can take it anymore. CODE OF HONOR is for Seagal fans only, and even then I'd still be cautious.

reviews: Visually stylish, but frequently dull  Maybe I went in with my expectations too high (mostly because of Tom Hiddleston), but after only really enjoying one of four films by Ben Wheatley so far, I'm beginning to think that maybe he isn't for me. That's not to say that HIGH-RISE isn't well-crafted, because it is. I just found it hard to really engage with it on a deeper level than the audiovisual components, and some of the performances. What really killed it for me, although there were a number of great moments to be had, was the slack pacing. It also didn't help that there wasn't any likeable characters to get behind other than Tom Hiddleston, who wasn't used as much I would have liked. The premise is rather simple: a large group of well-to-do people who live in a skyscraper descend into anarchy when power and water run short. Basically, the thesis is that, given a lack of necessary resources, society will revert to their more primitive instincts, and this takes the form of class warfare. Pretty accurate, if a little overdone by this point. J.G. Ballard's work has been successfully adapted before (although some might argue that point) with David Cronenberg's CRASH, but here the material didn't quite feel fresh, as social satires about class struggle have been done many times over. Keeping the film set in a retro-futuristic 1970's was a nice touch that worked, given the universality of the themes, but it seemed more like a stylistic choice than one organic to the story being told. The strongest elements the film were the production design, score, and the cinematography. All of these worked in tandem to give the effect of being slick and polished, with a detached "cool" factor that I liked. There was even one sequence which could have been its own music video. Ultimately, though, I found my mind frequently drifting, waiting to be jolted out of my boredom, but that never really happened to my satisfaction. HIGH-RISE isn't a bad movie, per se, but I will say that it wasn't for me.

reviews: Serves up a fitting conclusion to the series  THE HUNGER GAMES: MOCKINGJAY - PART 2 is a little better than it has a right to be. While I didn't mind the slower pacing of these last two installments, the fact that there was two final installments when there should have been one is already a strike against it. But that's Hollywood finance for you. Outside of the purely financial reasons for splitting the final book in two, this finale continued to explore the interesting political ideas discussed throughout the rest of the series, even if it was a discussion already had in other films, watered down here for the teenage masses. The principal cast continue to deliver effective performances, particularly Jennifer Lawrence and Donald Sutherland (who gets some of the film's best moments). The central concern seemed to be how the Rebels' and Capital upper echelons were essentially two sides of the same coin (pardon the pun). Again, while the notion that power can be exploited no matter what side of a conflict you're on is not new, I thought the film handled it well enough considering the pedigree of the source material. For those wondering about the action, like PART 1, there really isn't a lot of it although slightly more than last time. There were two big set-pieces, and both of them were suitably exciting. If your patience was tested during MOCKINGJAY PART 1, odds are you'll have the same issue here, but fans of the book series will probably see this no matter what (and probably already have). Other people might tune in out of obligation (like myself) just to see how things end. Ultimately, the story took some rather predictable turns, but nothing I couldn't live with. The only serious misstep was a coda that felt entirely unnecessary. In fact, 15 minutes could have been shorn from the end without detriment to the overall film or series. So, is THE HUNGER GAMES a great series? I would say no, but it breaks down political ideas for a younger audience in an effective way. If you've seen the previous three, of course watch this one; for everyone else, you'd be better served checking out BATTLE ROYALE 1 & 2.

reviews: A solid post-apocalyptic film  THE BOOK OF ELI is yet another entry in the well-populated post-apocalyptic genre and, to be honest, doesn't do a lot to distinguish itself from its brethren. What makes it an interesting watch are the stylistic choices, well-executed action, and committed performances from a stellar cast. The plot concerns Eli (mentioned by name only once), who is headed west with the last copy of the Bible (in the US, at least). On his journey he meets a warlord (Gary Oldman) who has been looking for the book and wants to use it for his own purposes. From a narrative standpoint, THE BOOK OF ELI keeps things very simple, and even the characters aren't too well-defined, being more archetypes than anything else. Of course, this is mostly fine as the film has higher ideas on its mind than just providing a cool story. There was some passing mention of what caused the world to be the way it is, and attempts at fleshing out the finer details of the world in the film, but nothing on the level of what George Miller did with the MAD MAX franchise. What holds the film together is Denzel Washington, who has made a career out of playing men of action (and, occasionally, few words). He plays Eli with the cool detachment required, but also imbues him with a sense of humor and humanity that makes him a little more relatable. Gary Oldman also does fine as the villain, but his motivations (as well as Eli's ultimate goal) remain unfortunately broad and vague. Mila Kunis is the weak spot in the cast, and she can't quite hold her own against such heavyweights. Outside of Denzel, where the film really shines is the style and action. Although the film has the same de-saturated color palette common in the genre, it contributed positively to the lived-in feeling of the world it depicted. Everything (and everyone) was appropriately grimy and dirty, as it should be when the world has suffered from nuclear war. I also thought there was creative work in the action sequences, particularly the first one in which Eli takes on a group of hijackers. It took place mostly in silhouette, which gave it a comic book feel. In fact, this film would make an excellent graphic novel. Still, the film is not without its problems. The biggest one is the pacing, which stays a little on the slow side. Granted, there are necessary moments where the characters can interact, but the combination of dour visuals and a slow pace didn't really mesh well. Also, as indicated earlier, the vagueness with which character motivation is treated was a bit disappointing. What saves the film from mediocrity is a great payoff in the last 20-25 minutes. I won't spoil anything here, but I will say that it makes a lot of sense if you know your Bible stories. Ultimately, THE BOOK OF ELI is a solid, if unspectacular, entry in its genre, but Denzel Washington's performance, inventive action sequences, and examination of religion's societal role make it worth your time.

reviews: Shakespeare by way of SHOWGIRLS  MOULIN ROUGE seems like one of those movies that you either love or hate, mostly because of Baz Luhrmann's style. I actually don't mind his style that much, having enjoyed AUSTRALIA and, to a lesser degree, THE GREAT GATSBY. Still, I wasn't even ten minutes into this and my head was already spinning. Thankfully, he doesn't keep the visual intensity cranked up to eleven the entire time, but a lot of time was spent in a hyperactive mode that gave me somewhat of a headache, while also laughing at the near-constant absurdity of what I was watching. If I had to describe it, and there are a number of ways to do so, it was like a fever dream or a roller-coaster that is perpetually on a downward course: exhilarating but also exhausting. The plot seemed almost an afterthought, with every romantic clichÃ© of the last 600 years or so being stuffed into a story of tragically doomed romance that was probably old hat when Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet. The acting, from an admittedly impressive roster of talented actors, was so over-the-top that it put primetime soap operas to shame. Just to give one example, John Leguizamo (as Toulouse-Lautrec?) sounded like Elmer Fudd with a lisp. Hopefully they had fun making this because I'd be ashamed to have this on my resume. Anyhow, acting and story aside, MOULIN ROUGE is a rather inventive (if derivative) movie. I would have never thought to set a musical in turn-of-the-century France yet use modern pop songs. The way in which they weave dozens of them in the dialogue is almost comical at times, but it worked for the most part. Where the film really shone, though, was the production design, sets and costumes. Other than paying the actors, this is probably where the most money was lavished, and it showed. Although confined to a few constructed sets, they were gorgeously realized and popping with detail. I don't know how this movie fared at the 2002 Oscars, but it probably got some well-deserved technical awards. Overall, MOULIN ROUGE was rather overwhelming, as if in a constant absinthe-induced delirium partially achieved through rapid-fire editing which gave it the feel of a two-hour music video. Still, Baz Luhrmann's commitment to overdoing every production element has some limited rewards and those are really what makes this worth watching, if only once.

reviews: An authentic and honest portrayal of the female experience  Where THE FALLING failed to engage me on an emotional level, GIRLHOOD provided that in spades. It tells the story of Marieme (Karidja Toure), a young girl on the cusp of becoming a woman. Like pretty much every person, she wants to find a place in the world and be happy, and the film is basically an exploration of how she tries to achieve those goals. The major thing standing in the way, one of the cold truths about how the real world works, is that not only is she a female, but a minority female as well. She goes through all of the usual difficulties in addition to ones unique to people of color. For instance, because of her low grades in junior high (or at least the French equivalent), an unseen school counselor suggests that she go to vocational school instead of moving on to lycee (high school), which Marieme rejects. Her path to self-realization is an arduous and emotionally difficult one in which she encounters sexism and abuse, but still manages to soldier on. Her story is the story of many young women and, for that reason, it should resonate with many people regardless of cultural boundaries. From a technical perspective, the production values were impeccable and all of the performances were perfect, with a degree of authenticity I haven't seen in a while. Every bit of dialogue felt realistic, and the actors were even able to convey a lot through equally deft physical performances. I also quite liked the score and soundtrack. The only reservation I have is that the narrative is a bit unbalanced in how much time it devotes to each phase of Marieme's "becoming," but this is otherwise a phenomenal effort from all involved. For whatever reason, this got no love from the Academy, but GIRLHOOD is definitely worth your time.

reviews: Cliched, pulpy source material elevated by fine filmmaking and performances  As spotty as Tony Scott's filmography was, it's easy to forget how good he could be. This is my first time seeing REVENGE and I must say that I was surprised by how emotionally involving and artfully directed it was, despite relying on a number of genre cliches. Kevin Costner plays Michael "Jay" Cochran, a 12-year Navy veteran who has just left the service and goes to see his friend, Tiburon Mendez (Anthony Quinn), in Mexico. While there, he ends up falling in love with Tibey's (as his friends call him) beautiful, young wife Miryea (Madeleine Stowe). When Tibey finds out about this, leaves Jay for dead and throws Miryea away in a whorehouse. The remainder of the film is Jay going back to rescue Miryea. Hopefully I haven't given too much away, but the film is 25 years old and there has to be a statute of limitations on spoilers, even if they're small. Since I liked more than I disliked, I'll just get the negative stuff out of the way first. I mentioned earlier that this film relies on genre cliches. One such example, and very key to establishing the central character relationship is the history shared by Tibey and Jay. Apparently, they were hunting buddies and Jay saved Tibey's life one time, so now Tibey is in debt to Jay. That's something that's been done to death in countless films before and since, but it wouldn't be such an issue if that wasn't the extent of it. It was just hard for me to buy that a Navy pilot would have it in so good with a Mexican power broker/kingpin. I also thought the romance that develops between Jay and Miryea was rather cliche, even if it was well-performed. And to be fair, this movie has some great performances in it. Kevin Costner was his usual likeable self, and veteran actor Anthony Quinn was great as his world-weary foil. Madeleine Stowe did fine, but isn't given much to do besides be the damsel in distress once confined to the whorehouse. Now, on to the positives (the rest). This is probably one of Tony Scott's best-directed films, and came a decade or so before he started using his much ripped-off MTV shooting style. There were some really artful shots, e.g., a fire being reflected in sunglasses or beautiful shots of the Mexican terrain. Even the sex scenes were shot well. I also really liked the score, which struck a fine balance between melancholy and tension. But most of all, and despite the cliched elements, the characters were well written and developed, and the performances really elevated the rather pulpy source material. Overall, REVENGE is an artful, occasionally thoughtful action thriller that probably deserves more attention than it got/currently gets. It might have a shaky dramatic foundation, but it's definitely worth seeing for what's built around and on top of it.

reviews: Compelling, but mostly on a visual/stylistic level  RUMBLE FISH is probably one of the less-seen films in Francis Ford Coppola's oeuvre, but I found it to be an eminently watchable, artsy gem that has a great sense of mood and style. The story revolves around Rusty James (Matt Dillon), a troubled teenager who finds it difficult living up to the reputation of his smarter older brother (Mickey Rourke). The main message I took from the film is that we too often look up to people for the wrong reasons, or idealize them without having a true sense of who they are. RUMBLE FISH explores youth through a dystopian lens, and Coppola conjures up dreamlike, occasionally borderline surreal, imagery to escort us through Rusty James' world. The film is in black and white, with a few instances of color for emphasis. Stylistically, this was a kind of cross between film noir, WEST SIDE STORY and a Michael Jackson video. In particular, an early fight sequence between Rusty and another character evoked the climactic fight in WEST SIDE STORY. In general, there was this balletic quality to the way the characters moved. When combined with Coppola's eloquent cinematography and an eclectic score, the effect is often hypnotic and always engrossing. That being said, the story itself meanders a bit too much and most of the performances (by young actors) were rather rough around the edges. Of course, part of that could have something to do with how the dialogue was post-synced. But still, RUMBLE FISH ranks pretty high among the most visually interesting films I've ever seen, even if the story and performances leave a bit to be desired.
