reviews: Hands down truest to the SPIRIT of the book- simply WONDERFUL  I read reviews, with interest and some perplexity.  I own this version and the one with [[ASIN:B01DOKAII6 William Hurt and Charlotte Gainsbourg]], love them both, for different reasons.  I hadn't read [[ASIN:B0082RHRHC the book]] in years but just did, to refresh my memory.  I had strong feelings about it.  I bookmarked passages that I found especially powerful or meaningful; I include them below- just skip them if you're not interested.***SPOILERS FOLLOW BUT NOT OF THE ENDING***  In my opinion the film version with William Hurt is by far the closest to the novel.  There are many aspects straight out of the book that are omitted in other versions, e.g., Jane's skill as an artist.  Much of the dialogue, Charlotte's prose, is word for word, intact therein.  As an aside though, something I've noted in general about adaptations of novels is that there isn't always a close correlation between cleaving to the narrative and dialogue of a novel, and the characterization (actors' affect, performances, context, etc), which highlights the influence the director, actors and others have on the finished product.  I read partly in reaction to criticisms relating to such issues in negative reviews.If I had to choose a favorite, this version, with Ciaran Hinds and Samantha Morton, would be it.  Why?  Because for me it seems truest to the SPIRIT of the book, especially in regards to the characterization.  I've long thought so re: Hinds as Mr. Rochester, and indeed, not only is he the spitting image as described by Bronte, but his behavior fits to a tee.  I highlighted in my kindle, was going to insert examples, but I won't bother (I'll include more substantive, interpersonal ones).  Read for yourself, regarding age (39), appearance (dark, grim), having a big head, his wide girth, demeanor, being out of control emotionally, capricious, unreasonable, even dangerous (there's a scene in the book where he comes very close to doing her real harm).  He's difficult, a BAD BOY, a type irresistible to some women, like catnip to a cat.  William Hurt's Rochester, whom I also like, is more aloof, controlled, enigmatic, etc.  Jane later meets St. John (pronounced "SIN-jin"), who is the polar opposite of Rochester, a fair Adonis, appearance-wise, but cold as a fish (except in his love of the Lord), and contrasts the two (much more so in the book).  (Incidentally, St. John's sister Diana is played by Elizabeth Garvie, who played Eliza Bennett in the wonderful 1980 BBC mini-series of [[ASIN:B000JIN3J8 Pride and Prejudice]].)  One reviewer said Hinds was more like the Beast in Beauty and the Beast than Mr. Rochester.  Actually, that's an excellent parallel, I thought the book quite suggestive of Beauty and the Beast.  I hasten to add I don't think Ciaran in the least homely, rather, gorgeous (my cup of tea so I'm biased, admittedly), but he's not afraid to grimace, scowl, cry, etc., in perfect character (and in other scenes, his large dark eyes dance, just as described by Bronte).And while I'm at it, I'd forgotten how MARVELOUS this book is.  It's incredible in its intelligence and arch feminism.  Would someone tell me why in every film version I can recall it's Mr. Rochester who puts out the fire in his bedroom, while a frightened Jane stands by helplessly?  In the novel it's JANE who puts out the fire, is unable to rouse Rochester (overcome by smoke) until AFTER she's extinguished the flames and saved his life.  This version is no different, but even so, Samantha Morton is likewise closest to the Jane of the novel.  At first I thought her a mite too personable, that she smiled too often, but in the novel Rochester mentions these aspects of her demeanor again and again.  I was so influenced by other film characterizations of this super-serious, SEVERE heroine that I'd forgotten her sass, her secret amusements, her good sense, her strong opinions, and most of all her passion and deep desire, as expressed in the novel, and Morton captures her perfectly. Indeed, Rochester observed early on "...you can laugh very merrily: believe me, you are not naturally austere, any more than I am naturally vicious."  Morton and Hinds have POTENT chemistry between them, too.Bronte published the book under a masculine-sounding nom de plume, but it didn't take long for the news to leak that it was penned by a woman.  She was then criticized for being "coarse", a euphemism for passionate or lurid.  As I recall this was the first book written in first person singular from a female protagonist's point of view, and readers were stunned by the desire and passion expressed by Jane Eyre, as well as the adult subject matter.  A middle aged man, describing his affairs and mistresses in detail to a young woman in his employ?  Unnerving, and yet- a very fine character study of two people, and the dynamic between them.  Example:Rochester:  "Is it better to drive a fellow-creature to despair than to transgress a mere human law, no man being injured by the breach? for you have neither relatives nor acquaintances whom you need fear to offend by living with me [in sin].â[Jane]:  This was true: and while he spoke my very conscience and reason turned traitors against me, and charged me with crime in resisting him.Â  They spoke almost as loud as Feeling: and that clamoured wildly.Â  âOh, comply!â it said.Â  âThink of his misery; think of his dangerâlook at his state when left alone; remember his headlong nature; consider the recklessness following on despairâsoothe him; save him; love him; tell him you love him and will be his.Â  Who in the world cares for you? Or who will be injured by what you do?Later that night:I would have got past Mr. Rochesterâs chamber without a pause; but my heart momentarily stopping its beat at that threshold, my foot was forced to stop also.Â  No sleep was there: the inmate was walking restlessly from wall to wall; and again and again he sighed while I listened.Â  There was a heavenâa temporary heavenâin this room for me, if I chose: I had but to go in and to sayâ âMr. Rochester, I will love you and live with you through life till death,â and a fount of rapture would spring to my lips.Â  I thought of this.Then:I skirted fields, and hedges, and lanes till after sunrise.Â  I believe it was a lovely summer morning: I know my shoes, which I had put on when I left the house, were soon wet with dew.Â  But I looked neither to rising sun, nor smiling sky, nor wakening nature.Â  He who is taken out to pass through a fair scene to the scaffold, thinks not of the flowers that smile on his road, but of the block and axe-edge; of the disseverment of bone and vein; of the grave gaping at the end: and I thought of drear flight and homeless wanderingâand oh! with agony I thought of what I left.Â  I could not help it.Â  I thought of him nowâin his roomâwatching the sunrise; hoping I should soon come to say I would stay with him and be HIS.Â  I longed to be his; I panted to return: it was not too late; I could yet spare him the bitter pang of bereavement.Â  As yet my flight, I was sure, was undiscovered.Â  I could go back and be his comforterâhis pride; his redeemer from misery, perhaps from ruin.Â  Oh, that fear of his self-abandonmentâfar worse than my abandonmentâhow it goaded me!Â  It was a barbed arrow-head in my breast; it tore me when I tried to extract it; it sickened me when remembrance thrust it farther in.Â  Birds began singing in brake and copse: birds were faithful to their mates; birds were emblems of love.Â  What was I?Â  In the midst of my pain of heart and frantic effort of principle, I abhorred myself.Â  I had no solace from self-approbation: none even from self-respect.Â  I had injuredâwoundedâleft my master.Â  I was hateful in my own eyes.(At the end I'll include another quote from this same section, shortly before Jane and Rochester part for the last time, in which he tells her of the effect she had on him at their first meeting.)  What a romantic and wonderful book, and one that cries out to be a mini-series because so MUCH has been left out of film versions to date (those I've seen, anyway).One critical reviewer said that this film version departs most significantly from the book.  I compared word for word the crowning glory of the film for me, the ending, which I find extremely moving and thrilling- brings me to tears and makes me want to cheer at the same time- and yes it does deviate, but again, I believe it is truest in spirit to the overall narrative.  Bronte is quite matter of fact at the end, but the import is there, beneath the subtlety.  For me this is in marked contrast to Pride and Prejudice with Keira Knightley, in which the film struck me as utterly untrue to the spirit of the novel- re: heavy breathing, heaving bosoms, passion and desire on steroids, NOTHING like Jane Austen's sensibilities.  Bronte, on the other hand, was nothing if not passionate.  Those who have loved another utterly will recognize themselves in these characters.  And a secondary theme I love in the narrative is that of love as salvation, that saves both, that engenders "the better angels" of their natures (as Abraham Lincoln said).My own feeling on differing film versions of favorite novels is that each (of the good ones anyway) rounds out the overall experience, fleshes out the book and complements the others.  Rarely does any one production capture all the nuances of a book- a different- deeper and broader- medium, duh.  Mini-series tend to do a better job, of course.  But even so, individual screenwriters, directors and actors bring their own foci and sensibilities to bear on the production.  This has been my experience many times, e.g., with the book [[ASIN:B016JMT5T4 North and South]] by Bronte's friend Elizabeth Gaskell, both the low-budget but splendid [[ASIN:B00H2QNTBW made-for-TV version from the 70s]] with a young Patrick Stewart, which is truer to the events of the book (and for me Stewart IS the iconic Thornton), and the gorgeous, atmospheric [[ASIN:B004EF65QA 2004 film]], which deviates substantially from the book but is inspired and inspiring nonetheless.  Likewise, for me the [[ASIN:B01DOKAII6 Gainsbourg-Hurt version]] of Jane Eyre and this Morton-Hinds one well complement each other, I watch them alternately.Here's one last excerpt from the book, from their first meeting, which suggests the spark of their personalities (both contrary!) and their instant attraction to each other (captured SO well by Hinds and Morton):As Jane reports, she's walking along at twilight, and a man on horseback speeds by-"...only a traveller taking the short cut to Millcote. He passed, and I went on; a few steps, and I turned: a sliding sound and an exclamation of âWhat the deuce is to do now?â and a clattering tumble arrested my attention. Man and horse were down; they had slipped on the sheet of ice which glazed the causeway."  She asks him if he's all right, he's rude and tells her to stand aside. She describes his appearance, behavior, and bad humor. He's clearly injured, she offers assistance several times, which he shuns dismissively, and she muses: "...if this stranger had smiled and been good-humoured to me when I addressed him; if he had put off my offer of assistance gaily and with thanks, I should have gone on my way and not felt any vocation to renew inquiries: but the frown, the roughness of the traveller, set me at my ease: I retained my station when he waved to me to go, and announced â âI cannot think of leaving you, sir, at so late an hour, in this solitary lane, till I see you are fit to mount your horse. â He looked at me when I said this; he had hardly turned his eyes in my direction before."Mr. Rochester describes this encounter later in the book, before they part for the last time:"...let me come to the point.Â  Last January, rid of all [my] mistressesâin a harsh, bitter frame of mind, the result of a useless, roving, lonely lifeâcorroded with disappointment, sourly disposed against all men, and especially against all womankind (for I began to regard the notion of an intellectual, faithful, loving woman as a mere dream), recalled by business, I came back to England.  I rode in sight of Thornfield Hall. Abhorred spot!  I expected no peace â no pleasure there. On a stile in Hay Lane I saw a quiet little figure sitting by itself.  I passed it as negligently as I did the willow opposite to it: I had no presentiment of what it would be to me; no inward warning that the arbitress of my life â my genius for good or evil â waited there in humble guise. I did not know it, even when, on the occasion of [the] accident, it came up and gravely offered me help. Childish and slender creature! It seemed as if a linnet had hopped onto my foot and proposed to bear me on its tiny wing.  I was surly; but the thing would NOT go: it stood by me with strange perseverance, and looked and spoke with a sort of authority.  I must be aided, and by that hand: and aided I was.When once I had pressed the frail shoulder, something new â a fresh sap and sense â stole into my frame. It was well I had learnt that this elf must return to me â that it belonged to my house down below â or I could not have felt it pass away from under my hand, and seen it vanish behind the dim hedge, without singular regret.  I heard you come home that night, Jane, though probably you were not aware that I thought of you or watched for you. The next day I observed you â myself unseen â for half- an- hour , while you played with AdÃ¨le in the gallery. It was a snowy day, I recollect, and you could not go out of doors. I was in my room; the door was ajar: I could both listen and watch.  AdÃ¨le claimed your outward attention for a while; yet I fancied your thoughts were elsewhere: but you were very patient with her, my little Jane; you talked to her and amused her a long time.When at last she left you, you lapsed at once into deep reverie: you betook yourself slowly to pace the gallery. Now and then, in passing a casement, you glanced out at the thick-falling snow; you listened to the sobbing wind, and again you paced gently on and dreamed. I think those day visions were not dark: there was a pleasurable illumination in your eye occasionally, a soft excitement in your aspect, which told of no bitter, bilious, hypochondriac brooding: your look revealed rather the sweet musings of youth when its spirit follows on willing wings the flight of Hope up and on to an ideal heaven. The voice of Mrs. Fairfax, speaking to a servant in the hall, wakened you: and how curiously you smiled to and at yourself, Janet ! There was much sense in your smile: it was very shrewd, and seemed to make light of your own abstraction. It seemed to say â âMy fine visions are all very well, but I must not forget they are absolutely unreal. I have a rosy sky and a green flowery Eden in my brain; but without, I am perfectly aware, lies at my feet a rough tract to travel, and around me gather black tempests to encounter.You ran downstairs and demanded of Mrs. Fairfax some occupation: the weekly house accounts to make up, or something of that sort, I think it was. I was vexed with you for getting out of my sight. Impatiently I waited for evening, when I might summon you to my presence.  [He sensed an] ...unusual... perfectly new character I suspected was yours: I desired to search it deeper and know it better.  YOU.  I was at once content and stimulated with what I saw: I liked what I had seen, and wished to see more.  [And]... I wondered what you thought of me, or if you ever thought of me, and resolved to find it out...And find out he does!  Though this feels relatively short (I was sorry when it ended), there's not a wasted word or scene in it- it succinctly expresses the novel's main themes and Bronte's passion.  And the ending is splendid.  Loved every minute of it- HIGHLY recommended.

reviews: Simply Wonderful  I LOVE this film.  It encapsulates every innermost yearning- for triumphing over circumstance, for being one's self while also of use in the world, finding one's purpose, expressing oneself creatively, and most of all, for finding true love.  I admit I dissolve into tears along with Beatrix up in her room after the momentous Christmas Party.  Simple but strangely perfect tale, and largely TRUE.  Besides being an early conservationist, what was left out of the story was the fact that Potter was a largely self-trained botanist (in mycology, the study of fungi) and based on her painstaking research developed a new theory of how fungi germinate and hybridize, largely ignored at the time due to her sex.  Her detailed botanical drawings and paintings are still used in the field today.  Extraordinary, as is this film.  The costumes, locales, cinematography, the music- all are splendid, up-close, intimate.  Everyone involved is letter perfect, and the chemistry between Zellweger and Ewan McGregor is potent.  One of my favorites.

reviews: Info GALORE on the Royal Family  I found this a little bizarre, but fascinating and informative.  All about the royal family, with it's lynch pin, the Queen Mother (formerly "Queen Elizabeth", namesake of the QE1, wife of King George the VI, or Bertie of [[ASIN:B004R36QUE The King's Speech]], and mother of the current Queen Elizabeth, namesake of the QE2).  This is ostensibly a biography of the Queen Mother, but it also details the stories of everyone close to her, i.e., the Royal Family for the last century- their proclivities, triumphs, scandals, etc.  What is evident about this documentary is that some of it must've been taken from a documentary on fashion and the Royal Family, because the jewels, gowns, and especially wedding dresses of nearly every royal wedding in the last 100 years are discussed.  Much is made of how the fashions reflected the times (for example, how the Queen Mother's HATS have evolved over the decades).  The photos and film clips are wonderful and I found the discussion lively and very interesting.Wonderful archival footage and interviews with people in the know.  A LOT is crammed into 100 minutes.  Though this will particularly tickle women's fancies, I think men who appreciate history and the historical record of the Royal's Family's participation in global affairs over the last 100 years will enjoy it too.  I watched this to find out how Queen Mary was related to the present Queen, and to the QE1, the Queen Mary, and the QE2, and I learned that and a WHOLE lot more.  Delves into the Queen Mother's personality in considerable depth- easy to see why she was so revered in Britain (a strong person, and quite a character).  ***SPOILERS FOLLOW*** For example, she persuaded her husband the King to visit America at the start of WWII- the first Royal visit EVER to America (by ANY monarch, and in this case, by those from the country from which America won its independence, incredible.  The Roosevelts served them hot dogs (!) and they and the King and Queen became friends as well as allies.  This documentary includes archival footage of the Queen Mother meeting everyone from Errol Flynn to the Beatles (lots of footage of Princess/Queen Elizabeth too, from infancy on).  Considerable detail on Prince Charles, who was very close to his Grandmother- his chief confidante and a kindred spirit, e.g., their shared favorite pastime was fly fishing.  The film also suggests involvement by his grandmother in his choice of Diana (Diana's grandmother was her long-time lady-in-waiting), and later in his affair with Camilla, too.  SCADS of information about the Royal Family from about 1900 on, beginning at the end of Queen Victoria's reign.  Highly recommended!

reviews: Succeeds on every level, simply wonderful  This is a balm to an aching heart, so shot thru with goodness, wonder, love, compassion and possibilities that it is restorative.  As good (if not better) than Hayao Miyasaki's work, which I also love (e.g. [[ASIN:B074121MFR Spirited Away]] and [[ASIN:B000CDGVOO Whisper of the Heart]]), or [[ASIN:B00TFVZXHA Song of the Sea]].  Shimmering, stunningly beautiful animation, lovely music, and inspired characterizations.  Even the subtitles are gorgeous, top notch, both visually (bright white on a black background) and lyrically/narratively.  But don't watch with the sound off- you must hear the character's voices and inflections.Natsume's Book of Friends began as a manga (comic book) series, serialized from 2005- present (the first 20 of the 22 volumes to date are available on Amazon in both paperback and kindle formats).  It was adapted into an animated (anime) TV series, broadcast in Japan for six seasons, in 2008, 2009, 2011, 2012, 2016 and 2017.  The first four seasons are available on Amazon Prime Video.  Both the manga and anime versions are critically acclaimed, and embody the best of Japanese sensibilities.  I often watch the NHK Network on PBS because these sensibilities are not only intriguing but therapeutic- attention to detail and a love of craftsmanship and excellence for its own sake, an animistic orientation towards all living things and the world as a living whole, and care and compassion for others' feelings and welfare (especially evident in their attitudes toward elders and the care thereof, ditto with pets).  Such values are embodied in Natsume's Book of Friends, the notion that even the smallest and seemingly least significant of beings (e.g., frogs, cats, children) are of of equal importance in the scheme of things.At the heart of this tale is a strange orphan boy's love for his deceased grandmother, who didn't quite fit into the world either.  The story jumps back and forth between two timelines, the boy's and his grandmother's at roughly the same age, in many ways pursuing twin paths.  Involved are supernatural spirits and forces, destiny, self-determination, discovering one's identity and purpose (along with going to high school and the pressures relating thereto).  Haunting and mysterious, there's also whimsy, humor, pathos, suspense, and INSPIRED storytelling.  Nothing is quite what it seems to be; the show channels the fears, hopes and dreams of a child's heart.  After one episode you may well be hooked like I was, I promptly bought all four seasons to savor.  Simply wonderful.

reviews: Narrative punch and superlative acting  Succeeds on so many levels and for so many reasons.  Steven Soderbergh did a masterful job of taking a story that could have easily dissolved into gratuitous farce/exploitation and imbuing it with humanity and compassion, along with narrative punch.  An acting tour de force by both Damon and Douglas, especially Douglas.  Douglas has Liberace's mannerisms, walk, movements etc. down to a T, astonishing.  Both actors play their roles with just the right amount of pathos and passion, flaws intact.  A powerful depiction of one person (a narcissist, likely) using another for his own selfish purposes, leaving him with nothing.  The supporting actors, e.g., Rob Lowe, Debbie Reynolds, Scott Bakula, Dan Akroyd, Bruce Ramsay (the jaded houseboy), all concerned, were superb.Add to this glitz, glamor, Liberace's phenomenal playing, and his charismatic persona (especially in the final scene), and it is plain to see why Liberace was a superstar.  I saw him perform in 1979 on the Queen Mary (I worked behind the scenes as a concierge and met him- an experience right up there with meeting John Carradine and Natalie Wood.  Thorsen was likely there, but I don't remember).  Liberace had his white baby grand piano lowered by crane onto the ship for use in his show (and possibly his Rolls Royce, though I may be imagining that).  He wore the white ermine robe with the yards long train, and absolutely wowed the crowd, the consummate showman.  A revealing and incisive look at a moment and place in time- if you like stories about Hollywood, celebrity, or gay culture in the drug-infused 70s and 80s, you may find this as provocative and fascinating as I did.  I recommend it for the acting alone- phenomenal.

reviews: Simply wonderful  I LOVE this film.  Gerard Depardieu shines as a seemingly simple man whose life is changed by making a new friend one day in the park. This is not saccharine in the least- subtle, utterly natural.  The lady in question, Margueritte, is reserved and formal, but they click, and form a friendship that will transform both their lives.  The glimpses of French village life and the countryside, the interactions of the townfolk, and most of all Depardieu, along with those close to him, are a delight.  I enjoy this film more with each viewing.  Laughter, tears, everything life is about.  Highly recommended.

reviews: For me, the flaws overshadowed its virtues  The good: the acting, the actors, some quirkiness.  The bad: awkward, woefully predictable, can see what's coming from the start of the movie.  I made the big mistake of purchasing before viewing- since I love David Stratthairn, and reincarnation/ love across time is one of my favorite themes, I thought I couldn't miss.  I was wrong. reviews: Meh and Spoiler Alert  Like many other reviewers I have experience with a family members with dementia and also have suffered multiple mild traumatic brain injuries (mtbi) myself. Alice's early symptoms were shockingly similar to my acute recovery from mtbi's. One family member had early onset Alzheimer's  while the other has elderly related dementia. The early onset is much more shocking and seems to progress far more quickly. Julianne Moore did a tremendous job as an individual experiencing and trying to manage this devastating disease. I felt that her part had depth and realism as did the part of her younger daughter. But the movie opens with this close-knit family and I expected to see myriad ways that they all experienced during the illness and how that interplayed between them as family members. There was hardly any of that. After about the first half hour, the son and oldest daughter were almost non existent in the film. The movie doesn't give you any sense as to why they just drop out of the story. So the viewer is left wondering if it's related to coping with disease or to life's business, or what? So their characters are not fleshed out at all. Spoiler alert - Alice's Alzheimer's is familial and one of these two have the gene. But that is never mentioned again. reviews: BEST movie of the year: Keanu, Halle & the team light it up.. A+ movie update  Just wow.  This movie hits it on all the right notes, from the cycle chase/katana scene (inspired by Villianess? good film)  to my favorite, the Moroccan sequence with Halle and the amazing dogs, to Laurence F to Keanu's superb weapon handling & badassery, this movie simply rocks.Fellow dog lovers will appreciate all the references; I was impressed by Halle's phenomenal stunt work with them in Morocco, plus Halle's grit, beauty & strength (and the water bottle scene in the desert was lol).Keanu is intense, focused and outstanding as always -- you always deliver, thanks.  Totally believable weapon handling, props for taking time to train, you're authentic.  Plus when I look up the word "badass" in the dictionary, there you are, lol.  Well done.  Good chemistry with Halle, and team fight choreography.  I lol at the best line, eg Sophie "he shot my dog", Keanu deadpans "I get it".  :pThis is one of those rare movies I've watched over and over again, it's packed with creative action sequences.  The fight scene in Morocco I've watched eight times; it rocks (runtime at minute 57).Writing, visual fx, fight choreography, set design, the new Adjudicator (Asia you rocked; fan from Billions; you're compelling; strong), it's all great.Glad the team put so much work into this.  Brilliant directing, fast paced & intense.  Writing didn't get in the way of the acting.  Watching behind-the-scenes youtube videos, Keanu & Halle thankfully put in long hours to prep for this, and it shows.  Gritty, authentic and unique scenes makes this a wonderfully crafted movie.If I were to improve it I'd cut the entire director/ah role (convoluted, slowed the pacing; Judi Dench would've been better) & replace with more Laurence F/bowery; he's excellent.  In the intro library scene the villian was boring af, a female badass assassin would've been better, like Harley Quinn.  The 2nd fight scene w/asian gang was a bit too long.  And the entire ballet/director scene was truly boring af & a waste; the high table backstory could've been written much better.The scenes with phone operators updating Wick's status added a nice urgent touch, 50s retro style done perfectly (way better than a modern digital set; liked the rotary phones/chalkboard etc, brilliant set design).  The concierge guy & hotel manager also delivered solid, believable performances.Mark D was Great as Zero, a super bad-guy for Keanu to fight, very human + lethal; you delivered one of the best villian character performances I've ever seen, being both ruthless and fan of John Wick, nice balancing act.  Movies are only as good as their heroes/villians, and you crushed it.  Genuinely liked your character.  You made a sympathetic multi-layer bad guy who is genuinely interesting.  Funny sitting on sofa scene.  Solid martial arts in final glassroom fight scene.  Bravo.I'm sure the cast & crew read all these reviews ... many thanks to all of you for putting in the hard work to make this a total kickass movie; I appreciate your talent.  Longtime fan of Keanu, Halle and Laurence -- thank you!Ken Calhoun, founderTradeMasteryp.s. if you ever need an incredibly handsome famous stock trader / sax player in a bit role in a future film, it would be my honor, and yes I'm serious :)p.p.s. grateful to Finally see a great film recently, you folks have my thanks for doing it right.  A+

reviews: Idris and Matthew shine, in a movie that just plain left too much on the cutting room floor.  Point one:  Idris Elba NAILED it.He really showed his chops again, proving countless fans who worried about the image (myself included) dead wrong.Matthew solidly pulled off his character, as well.  Just the right amount of charismatic and creepy.The problem is the film itself.  I love that they didn't try to stick to the story, because it would have been impossible.  That said, by the time the credits are done scrolling, you end up with a movie that's about as long as a television drama episode.  There's nowhere near enough time to explore the events and characters here.That was always King's strength; delving (sometimes perhaps a little too deeply) into the minds and motivations of his creations.  Without Idris helming this picture, the gunslinger would have fallen flat.  He pretty much saved the script in concert with Matthew, as there is very, VERY little script to work with.I'd love to see the one-page screenplay behind this.  The producer really dropped the ball when bringing the team together here.  He nailed the actors, but neglected everything else.Should you watch this?Absolutely, if you've got the cash for a fun evening romp through a strange fantasy/sci-fi/drama.  Just don't expect the book (which is honestly a good thing, because they'd have butchered it) and don't expect high cinema.Also, don't expect to be entertained very long.  This movie should have had another hour to explore it's plot.  I don't feel monetarily cheated, but I do feel creatively cheated. reviews: Fun and Fascinating Travel Series  I freely admit to being a Josh Gates fan, both for his quirky sense of humor and his willingness to go to extremes to take us to exotic locations in search of mysteries both great and small. I also appreciate his open-minded skepticism, something I think a lot of other reviewers of his various shows often overlook. Sure, he goes in search of some pretty out-there things, but in spite of his frequent enthusiasm for the search, he also displays a healthy skepticism that helps ground things.Expedition Unknown, as a whole, is an excellent series. Some people complain he never finds anything, but let's be serious for a moment -- many of the things he sets out in search of have been the subject of decades if not centuries of dedicated searching. It would be completely unrealistic to expect Josh to come along and suddenly solve or find everything each episode. That's not the point, anyway. What makes Expedition Unknown both fun and interesting is the journey, not the destination; that is to say, it is the places he goes, the people he meets, and the inevitable trouble he gets into that makes the show so enjoyable for me. While I would to see him find more, I am perfectly content with just enjoying the journey for its own merits. Any new or even potential discoveries are just icing on the cake.This new season starts out with a bang by tackling the infamous Dyatlov Expedition. The mere fact Josh and is crew are willing to go so far out into the icy heights of the Urals attests to their dedication to their show and their craft.  That they chose to do so by following the actual path taken by the Dyatlov Nine rather than just flying in by helicopter only underscores how willing this show is to explore its mysteries as thoroughly as possible. Great stuff! In all seriousness, though, if you go into this show viewing it as a travel show that focuses on mysteries and the unknown, it is incredible. If you expect a series documentary, you'll be disappointed and likewise, if you expect just another run-of-the-mill ghost/alien/monster-hunting show, you'll also be disappointed. Expedition Unknown undeniably has elements of both, but it combines them to create a travel series that serves to take us all on a wonderful adventure to faraway lands with a healthy focus on location and culture, and in the end that's what matters the most to me.

reviews: Bad  I went into this movie with mediocre expectations.  It's hard to bring an animated staple of my youth to life in a live action representation.  I was prepared to be forgiving, if it didn't live up to the original film, because there are certainly a lot of challenges to make something like this work.  I did however, expect Disney to put their best foot forward and create a nostalgic experience for the die hard fans, as well as an entertaining and well made remake for new viewers experiencing this story for the first time.Sadly, I was sorely disappointed, even with my low expectations.  The production was sloppy, the direction was horrible, and I can't even begin to understand what they were thinking when they cast this thing.  I liked the idea of Will Smith as the genie, in concept.  But, in practice, it was just BAD.  Every actor in this movie was horrible.  The dialogue, the acrobatics, and sadly, the Genie.  I respect Will Smith tremendously as an actor, but this was just sad.  I can only assume that the blame for his lack of character falls upon the director and producers.  The reason for the animated films success, lies in the fact that Robin Williams was given a great deal of room to bring his personality to the Genie.  Instead of trying to cut and paste Robin's rendition of the Genie into the movie via Will Smith, I would have been more pleased to see Will bring more of his own magic to the character.  At first glance, the set design seems to be above par, as well as the wardrobe, But if you're watching closely, it's easy to see where the set designers cut corners.  In fact, there only seem to be a few sets in the entire production that weren't completely green screened. Even the CG was substandard, which should have fallen within Disney's wheelhouse.  While this reboot may be a good distraction for your toddlers, with all it's pretty light shows and colorful outfits, it lacks the heart of the original.  I doubt that you or your children will look back fondly on this adaptation in 25 years the way that most of us do for the original.

reviews: Anachronisms, anachronisms, anachronisms...  This is a period piece about a Soviet spy set in 1985 and that must end prior to August 1991, since that's when the Soviet Union fell and since the Soviet Union still remains unfallen at the end of the movie, despite the fact that doing the math according to the timelines given in the film would seem indicate the movie ends in the spring of 1992. But that's not actually one of the anachronisms of which I speak.Towards the very beginning of the movie, we see Anna in a squalid public housing apartment in Moscow that she shares with her boyfriend in 1987. The movie is very non-linear, jumping back and forth in time with flashbacks and flashforwards to a dizzying degree, probably to try and distract from its many plot holes, but these are also not the anachronisms of which I speak. In that 1987 scene, Anna hasn't yet been recruited by the KGB and is an unemployed junkie, just like her boyfriend. She's sitting at the dining room table on her boyfriend's slim laptop PC with a color monitor running Windows or some Windows-like operating system and is using wi-fi and a browser to wirelessly access the Soviet Union's Navy's website to complete an online application to join the Soviet Navy. So how do a pair of lowlife junkies have a laptop that's still 13 years away from being invented and have a wi-fi router that's at least 15 years away from being at all commonplace to access a website that never existed, not just because the USSR never made it but because the Web itself wouldn't become public until six years later in April 1993, two years after the Soviet Union ceased to exist? It's ridiculous.That's just the start of the anachronisms of which I speak.In 1990, she breaks into the security room of a Paris hotel which has all its surveillance monitors networked on an ethernet server that wouldn't come out until 2001 and steals a removable hard drive that wouldn't be invented for 20 more years.In 1990, long before anyone was walking around with cell phones, back when cell phones were those enormous bricks, so obscenely expensive to use only the richest people had them, and had coverage so poor coverage was not existent most places and at best spotty in the biggest cities, but in Anna cell phones are so common in 1990 that she not only is able to pick pocket a cell phone from the first random person she passes back when cell phones didn't even fit in pockets, the one she pick pockets is a Nokia candy-bar cell phone that wouldn't be invented for another 10 years, which she then uses to call her handler, who answers using a Motorola flip phone that wouldn't come out until 1996.It goes on and on. It's like the makers of the movie were people who had no contextual idea about what technology developed when and didn't bother to look it up and didn't even bother to check the year the vintage props they'd purchased were made to make sure they weren't made AFTER the time period of the movie. What's more, none of it was necessary, like they could've had her filling out the Navy application on paper, could've had her pull a video tape out of a VCR recording the security camera footage, and could've had her use a pay phone to call her handler who could've answered a landline at his desk instead of at a dinner table.I could maybe suspend my disbelief of how she repeatedly killed dozens upon dozens of assassins that would appear out of nowhere and everywhere in absolutely unbelievable onslaughts that were like the movie Kill Bill had a baby with a first-person shooter video game. I could maybe overlook the cliche characters and cliche plot filled with plot holes because that's just the kind of action movie this is. I could maybe even get past the very cringey and painfully implausible ending where she meets up with her KGB handler and CIA handlers, both of whom she's suddenly portrayed as being deeply in love when we've seen no such emotional interchange between them to that point save for a couple of seemingly meaningless and gratuitous sex scenes, leading to maybe the most ridiculous stand-off I've ever seen in a movie. But what I could not get past, could never get past, is anachronism after anachronism after anachronism.I myself would only give two stars, but since anyone born after 1985 would probably not notice the many, many, many, many anachronisms and since that's its target audience, I figure to them, it's a 3-star action flick, it's plot holes, bad writing, implausible action scenes, unfounded emotionality, cliche characters, and cringey ending being par for the course for such films-- average, so an average rating.

reviews: A mostly faithful adaptation of Wyndham's short story of the same name  I've read most of John Wyndham's stories, starting with his early SF novel the Day of the Triffids, and moving on to his best novel (in my opinion), Rebirth, and from there to his other novels and short story collections.  I had no idea his short story Random Quest had been made into a (TV) movie until I happened onto it by accident on Amazon.The short story was published decades ago, and is one I've read several times (what can I say... I like Wyndham's writings). Many of Wyndham's stories have the theme of soul-mates separated by time, space or quantum incidents, somehow reconnecting and finding each other again.  This one is true to form.The main weakness in the movie version is the pseudo-science, which it could have done without: not so much the notion of parallel worlds or lives, which is well established as an implication of quantum physics, but the explanation about black holes being the mechanism for shifting a character from one "universe" to another -- a little silly notion since (1) a black hole anywhere in the proximity of the Earth would destroy it, and (2) the main character's consciousness, rather than his physical body, is what moves between realities.  Better not to address the cause, than to garble it up with transparently silly explanations.Random Quest (the movie) is reasonably good. It's not perfect; the narrative could be tighter and more sharply focused.  One obvious important plot point was entirely omitted.  Still it's a mostly faithful adaptation of Wyndham's story.  The main thing it lacks is the intense, almost neurotic motivation the main character in the short story had that kept him searching for Otillie: his deep, almost schizoid sense that she really was his soul mate, that his life wouldn't be complete without her.  The movie also misses the set-up, that he's been searching for months and has almost no hope of finding her again. So the ending, though cute, doesn't have a lot of impact.Still it's a fun little movie.  Low budget, obviously made for TV... the low key British public television equivalent of an old Twilight Zone episode. If you have Amazon Prime and can watch it for free, by all means do so.

The rest of the description leads you to believe this is just another courtroom drama of a wrongly accused man.  After watching almost everything else of interest on the IMdB channel we, under desperation, decided to give this a try.  At first it looked good enough to stay with it.  Good photography and good acting always help, but the plot needs to be up to snuff or the best actors in the world cannot save it.  In this case the plot weakens progressively as you move forward.  There are no twists to hold your interest but there is plenty of predictability.  You can guess the ending so there's no need for a spoiler.  This film falls flat for the very same reason that most Christian-based films fail.  They rely too much on the word of God and not enough on the fundamentals of film making or story telling.  They believe that all they have to do is sprinkle in a few Gospel verses into the script and mention God or any one of his many other names and there have been too many to count over the centuries.  In this film the writers think they have been creative and witty to refer to God by the name of Papa.  I found it to be trite and over simplified.  It's much like today's Gospel songs with one hook phrase repeated over and over and over compared to yesterdays Hymns with 3, 4 and 5 verses plus a chorus.  Today's Christians don't like complexity and so this film follows that trend - much to it's own demise.Because it has some good momentes and the acting is not to bad, I can't give it a 1-star rating but it's certainly not in the 5-star class either so I settled for a mediocre score.

reviews: Wonderful Surprise Movie Not normally Found in the Mainstream Sources  Before I write a review I always read the majority of other reviews already published.  I always read 100% of both the 1-star and 5-star reviews and skim those in the middle so that I won't repeat something that has already been covered.  What I found in the 1-star reviewers comments was an overabundance of un-validated reviews and a lot that are not  even reviews at all but rather just statements of discontent.  Professional reviewers give you a reason for their disappointment - a qualification for a low rating.  Amatures just dis the film with no justification.What I liked about this film is the amount of differences it has with other films in this genre.  The inclusion of several Native American actors that are not usually cast was a treat.  Graham Greene always adds an element of humor even when he is not trying to be funny.  While this film is not necessarily trying to be a comedy, there are comedic moments that help keep interest flowing.  A lower than normal budget makes this just a bit "campy".  With just a bit more capital influx this could have become a seasonal classic.One of the best surprises for me the first time watching was the discovery of singer Rita Coolidge cast in a pivotal role.  I've been a Rita Coolidge fan since her first LP in 1971.  I've always thought she was a gorgeous woman with an angelic voice comparable to none.  Her acting ability in Billy and the Kid was probably under-directed.  In this film however she looks as natural in the role as if she is playing herself interacting with her own daughter. My only complaint here is that she didn't have as much On-Screen time as I would have liked to see.

reviews: Most misleading title and description on Amazon  THANK YOU to all the 1-star reviewers who gave me a heads up.THREE MEN IN A TUB would be a more accurate title!  Even though there are about 8 to 10 men in this lifeboat, this movie has nothing to do with Greyhounds or Wolfpacks and very little to do with the Atlantic ocean.First you need to know that if you are American or any other nationality (other than British) you might have a hard time following the dialogue.  Bad audio habits from the film crew and bad diction and mumbling from the cast make it very difficult to understand.Next, you need to understand the style of movie making in England in the 1950s.  First, most of the cast are far to old to be serving in the Navy or Merchant Marines during WWII.  Some of them may have been too old to serve in the HOME GUARD which was made up of all the left-overs (those who could not serve any other place).  Next, most of the movie happens with the cast in the lifeboat.  As small as it is, you can only see about 4 men at a time on camera.  So I am assuming that every time the camera angle shifted from stem to stern, 4 of the cast had to jump out to make room for the camera crew.  Not to worry though, they would have jumped out to a stage floor, not the cold, cruel and unforgiving Atlantic....all of that was dubbed in via green screen (in otherwords, not much reality on screen).  Without the reality of the terror, the fright, the uncertainty of the Atlantic we're left with just the Actor's ability to convey those emotions.  Unfortunately, this acting crew did nothing to aid that outcome.After just a few minutes my mind got very taxed at trying so hard to focus on what was being said that I mentally tuned it out and started looking for something else to watch.  At about 10 minutes of having the sound in the background, I realized that it too was over-taxing my brain and was so relieved when I remembered I had a MUTE button.  At 25 minutes, not much had changed on screen - still 3 men in a tub...so OFF it went.  Glad I didn't waste any more time with it.  Thanks again 1-star people.

reviews: Not as Entertaining as good movies goe  For all those 1-star reviewers who said:, "It didn't happen this way": If you want it to be real, you should be watching a documentary.  Movies are for entertainment.  Movies are for expanding the reality.  Movies allow the characters to get away with more than they ever could in real life.  The same things you say about this movie could also be said about movies like: "The Battle of Britan", "The Great Escape", and "Dunkirk".That being said, I still gave this movie only 1 star because I can't stand the poor cinematography.  The constant jerking of the camera back and forth and zooming in/out is a poor excuse for trying to simulate what one sees when they dart their eyes back and forth.  It doesn't translate to the same thing.  What we see with our eyes cannot now or ever be duplicaed with a single lens camera.  What we, the viewers, get when the camera operator attempts this effect is a "Hard-to-Watch" picture bouncing around a flat screen and the wider the screen, the worse the effect and the harder it is to watch.  The human eyes can process depth perception instantaneously. The camera cannot.  Even with Zoom, the camera is limited to the end result of a picture on a flat screen.I knew instantly when this film began that if I attempted to watch, I'd end up with a migraine headache from the eye strain.  This is why it get's only 1 star from me

After we watched the first episode, they waned more. They wanted toys and books, they wanted to watch the movies with me. It was just like 1980 all over again when i stood in line to watch Empire Strikes Back.But that's enough of my nostalgia. The episodes are fun. Sure they have their problems, but honestly, what in Star Wars doesn't? Watching the characters come together has been fun and interesting. Seeing all of the nods to Ralph McQuarrie's original vision of Star Wars, and the Kenner toys, and even the original Star Tours attraction at Disneyland are fun. The action is spot on for grabbing the attention of younger kids, it's well conceived and animated. The character models pull in elements of Disney Characters that the kids know as well as Star Wars characters that the parents know.At its heart, it is exactly what it should be to carry on the tradition of the original Star Wars. Fans believe that they are so much more sophisticated and need more "adult" entertainment from the show, but that's not what they are nostalgic for. reviews: Your mobile phone "knows" your secrets!.  Everyone has something they want to keep secret.  Some part of their lives that they would not want others to know about.  Whoever had knowledge of that secret and has the ability to reveal or to conceal it will have power over others.  Gaining control over the mobile phone of a modern, socially-connected person could allow someone access to not only sensitive information, but also to use the device's microphone and camera to spy on that person. That is the premise of this thoroughly modern suspense thriller from the Netherlands.Anna (Hannah Hoekstra) is a college student who is majoring in psychology.  She has a lot going on in her life. Naturally, the professor confiscates the phone and asks Anna to stop by his office later to pick it up.In the next scene, we see two phones on the teacher's desk. IRIS then proceeds to dig into the man's personal life and proceeds to destroy it.As the plot progresses, Iris starts taking media files from Anna's mobile and distributes them to her social connections. From time to time, additional content will play on the mobile phone's display while the movie is playing.  This could be a different camera angle on the same scene playing on TV, text messages being transmitted by the characters, news flash, and extra scenes.  The "second screen" experience did not detract from the enjoyment of the film in any way. Mobile phones are now being steadily embraced in higher education, as lessons and course content are being created to integrate mobile devices in the classrooms. If "Game of Thrones" shy away from "comfort fiction", then this show certainly is a departure from the normal reality TV shows out there.This is a show that should be made available to health educators out there.  Perhaps even to high school science classes.  Dan Riskin presents his commentaries in a very informative manner.  There's a lot to be learned from these episodes.
